<document>
<title>Turning Red</title>
<fragment>

The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. Liu said that working on a feature film was "a dream come true".[14] By November 26, 2018, Shi confirmed that the film was in the early stages of development, with the story still being worked on, and that "[she is] really excited to play in this new 90-minute film format".[15] The title *Turning Red* was finalized by December 10, 2020.[16][17] According to Morris, *Turning Red* had one of the fastest development times of a Pixar feature film, taking only four years to complete.[13]



### Casting

<fragment>

Shi, who previously directed the short film *Bao* (2018), developed the film based on her experiences growing up in Toronto. She pitched three concepts, including *Turning Red*, to Pixar in October 2017. Development began in May 2018 when Shi was announced as writer and director of a full-length film; several Pixar animators visited locations around Northern California gathering inspiration and visual references. The design and animation were inspired by anime works. To capture these anime influences, hand-drawn 2D animated effects were added atop Pixar's 3D animation. Development on *Turning Red* lasted for four years, on an approximate $175 million budget, becoming the fastest production for a Pixar film. Ludwig Göransson composed the film's musical score for his first animated film, with Billie Eilish and Finneas O'Connell writing original songs for the film.


</fragment>

Shi wrote an animated webcomic series titled *My Food Fantasies* in 2014, in which she drew "outlandish" situations involving food.[15] Shi later said that she developed her interest in writing stories about food while making *My Food Fantasies*.[16] The first feature film she worked on with Pixar was *Inside Out* (2015), on which she served as a storyboard artist.[10] After briefly working on *The Good Dinosaur*, Shi began working on *Toy Story 4* in 2015.[12] She also drew storyboards for the 2018 film *Incredibles 2*, where she worked on a sequence featuring the characters Jack-Jack and Edna Mode.[17]

<title>Turning Red</title>
<fragment>

The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. Liu said that working on a feature film was "a dream come true".[14] By November 26, 2018, Shi confirmed that the film was in the early stages of development, with the story still being worked on, and that "[she is] really excited to play in this new 90-minute film format".[15] The title *Turning Red* was finalized by December 10, 2020.[16][17] According to Morris, *Turning Red* had one of the fastest development times of a Pixar feature film, taking only four years to complete.[13]

Shi, who previously directed the short film *Bao* (2018), developed the film based on her experiences growing up in Toronto. The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. Liu said that working on a feature film was "a dream come true".[14] By November 26, 2018, Shi confirmed that the film was in the early stages of development, with the story still being worked on, and that "[she is] really excited to play in this new 90-minute film format".[15] The title *Turning Red* was finalized by December 10, 2020.[16][17] According to Morris, *Turning Red* had one of the fastest development times of a Pixar feature film, taking only four years to complete.[13]

<title>Bao</title>
<content>
![](image)

Look up ***bao*** in Wiktionary, the free dictionary.

**Bao,** also known as **baozi**, is a type of Chinese dumpling made of steamed or baked bun with fillings.


**Bao** or **BAO** may also refer to:




## Cuisine

[edit]

* Gua bao, steamed clam-shaped bun sandwiched with meat and condiments originating from Fujian, China
* Bánh bao, Vietnamese dumpling with pork meat inside, derived from the Chinese bao
* Bao stir-frying, a high heat variant of the Chinese stir frying technique


## People

[edit]

* Bao (surname), a common pronunciation for some Chinese surnames, such as 包 and 鮑
	+ Bao Zheng or Lord Bao, Chinese judge of Song China
		- Justice Bao (disambiguation)
* Bao (musician), Vietnamese-American musician


## Acronyms

[edit]

* Baccalaureus in Arte Obstetricia, Bachelor of Obstetrics, a medical degree unique to Ireland
* Baryon acoustic oscillations, in physical cosmology
* *Batman: Arkham Origins*

A driving motivation for Shi's desire to tell the story in *Bao* was her experiences of being Asian in a country with lack of Asian-American media. Her influences include those derived from having grown up watching Asian films and animation, including those of Studio Ghibli. Initially Shi was worried that the ending was too dark, and would be out of place for a Pixar film, which prompted her to write a watered down version. However, when she pitched it to her mentor, Pete Docter, who became an executive producer on *Bao*, he encouraged Shi to pitch the darker version, and stay true to her original idea and preferred style, saying, "Don't be afraid to push it, be as culturally specific as you want it to be."[7]

In 1984, Sheridan student Jon Minnis[13] created the short animation piece *Charade.* The five-minute film was animated by Minnis with Pantone markers on paper during a single three-month summer term at Sheridan College. The film won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film at the 57th Academy Awards.[14][15] As Sheridan's animation department continued to grow, it produced hundreds of animators into Canadian and international studios, at one point in 1996 being called "the Harvard of animation schools" on "a worldwide basis" by animator Michael Hirsh. A significant number of graduates have held key positions at Walt Disney Animation Studios, Don Bluth Productions, Pixar Animation Studios, and DreamWorks Animation, both for traditional and CGI animation.[7] Sheridan graduates include seven Academy Award nominees and two winners,[16][17][18] including Domee Shi, the first woman to direct a Pixar animated short.[19][20]

<fragment>

Although *Bao* was approved for production in 2015, Shi knew it would be a long and uncertain journey, equating shorts films to an indie wing of Pixar, which would have to borrow people who are free for a couple weeks at a time in between feature films. *Bao* thus had to be worked on more slowly, creatively and flexibly, with the production only finding out that it would be paired with *Incredibles 2* a year before that film's release. Shi found the pairing thematically appropriate, as both films, in her view, celebrated mothers. Fitting her story into the eight-minute running time forced Shi to be economical with the shots of food.[7]


Shi viewed the film as an example of stories Pixar had come to embrace featuring greater diversity and cultural perspectives, a road that had been paved by previous Pixar films including the Pixar short, *Sanjay's Super Team* and the 2017 feature film *Coco*.[9]

**Domee Shi** (/ˈdoʊmi/;[1] Chinese: 石之予; pinyin: *Shí Zhīyǔ*; born 8 September 1989)[2][3] is a Canadian film director and screenwriter. She directed the 2018 short film *Bao* and the 2022 feature film *Turning Red*, becoming the first woman to direct a short film and then the first woman with sole director's credit on a feature film for Pixar.[4][5]


Shi began working for Pixar in 2011 as a storyboard artist, contributing to multiple films, including *Inside Out* (2015), *Incredibles 2* (2018), and *Toy Story 4* (2019).

### *A Spark Story*

[edit]

Main article: A Spark Story

On January 29, 2020, Disney announced that an untitled documentary series focusing on the *SparkShorts* series was in development for Disney+.[21] The series, which provided "an immersive look at the next generation of Pixar filmmaker[s]", was executive-produced by Brian McGinn, Jason Sterman and David Gelb.[21] On July 21, 2021, it was reported that the project was being redeveloped as a docu-film under the name *A Spark Story*, with McGinn, Sterman, and Gelb producing.[9] Sterman also directed the film alongside Leanne Dare.[9] Pixar produced the project alongside Supper Club.[9] The documentary, charting the production of then-recent *SparkShorts* *Twenty Something* and *Nona*, was released on September 24, 2021.[22]

## 皮克斯动画故事长片的复杂创作过程

### 1. 整体协作哲学

皮克斯以其独特的"脑托会”（Braintrust）协作过程而闻名，这是一个由经验丰富的导演、编剧和创意人员组成的团队，定期审阅和提供反馈。这种协作文化确保了每部影片都经过多轮创意打磨：

- **集体智慧驱动**：不同于单一导演主导的模式，皮克斯强调团队的集体智慧
- **内部反馈循环**：脑托会成员以建设性方式互相提供坦诚反馈
- **多次迭代**：故事会经历反复的修改和完善过程

### 2. 从短片到长片的技能培养路径

从史兆予的经历可以看出，皮克斯有明确的人才培养体系：

**短片的独立创作环境**：
- 短片被比作皮克斯的"独立分支"
- 史兆予描述短片制作过程：工作人员只能"借用那些在故事长片之间有几周空闲时间的人"
- 短片制作需要"更缓慢、更创造性、更灵活"的工作方式

**技能积累与信任建立**：
- 史兆予从2011年开始在皮克斯担任故事板艺术家
- 参与了《头脑特工队》(2015)、《超人总动员2》(2018)、《玩具总动员4》(2019)等多部影片
- 通过短片《包》(2018)证明了导演能力，获得奥斯卡最佳动画短片奖

### 3. 长片制作的分层创新体系

### SparkShorts项目的发展意义：

**个人故事的孵化器**：
- SparkShorts允许员工讲述"个人故事"
- 这些短片成为新导演和创意人才的试验场
- 如《Purl》、《Smash and Grab》等作品探索了不同于传统皮克斯风格的主题

### 4. 创意的有机组织结构

史兆予的《青春变形记》展现了皮克斯如何协调创新：

**全女性领导团队**：
- 史兆予提到导演、编剧、制作设计等核心创意职位首次全部由女性担任
- 皮克斯CEO吉姆·莫里斯表示这" happened very organically"（非常自然地发生了），而非刻意为之
- 这个团队被报道为"皮克斯有史以来制作效率最高的影片之一"

**快速开发过程**：
- 《青春变形记》仅用四年完成，是皮克斯"开发速度最快的故事长片之一"
- 从2018年5月宣布史兆予担任导演，到2022年上映，展现了相对快速的制作周期

### 5. 文化多样性的融入

皮克斯逐渐拥抱多元文化视角：

**递进式的文化包容**：
- 史兆予认为《包》是皮克斯拥抱多样性和文化视角的例子
- 她提到这个道路由之前的《桑杰的超级战队》和《寻梦环游记》（2017）铺平
- 这个转变反映了皮克斯从 predominantly 西方视角向全球多元文化叙事的演进

### 6. 技术与创意的平衡

从《包》的创作过程可以看出技术限制如何推动创意：

**限制激发创意**：
- 《包》只有八分钟的片长，迫使史兆予"在食物的镜头上精打细算"
- 短片制作需要在技术限制下找到创造性解决方案
- "慢动作"的动画制作过程要求更高的精确度和规划

### 7. 多代际的经验传承

皮克斯通过不同项目维持创意连续性：

**跨项目经验传承**：
- 短片制作团队从故事长片项目中"借用"人员
- 这种人员流动确保了经验在公司内部传承
- 新导演可以通过短片项目获得宝贵经验，为长片做准备

## 总结：平衡体系的复杂性和卓越性

皮克斯的协作创作过程是一个精密的平衡系统：

1. **个体创造力与集体智慧的平衡**：既鼓励个人故事讲述，又通过脑托会等机制确保质量
2. **创新与传统的平衡**：通过SparkShorts等项目尝试新风格，同时维持皮克斯核心质量标准
3. **速度与质量的平衡**：《青春变形记》的快速开发并不牺牲品质，反而效率更高
4. **多样性与统一性的平衡**：拥抱多元文化叙事的同时保持皮克斯动画的美学统一性

这种复杂协作过程的成功在于各个元素之间的协调与平衡，使皮克斯能够在保持高水平品质的同时，不断推出创新且具有文化意义的作品。史兆予从短片导演到长片导演的成长轨迹，充分体现了皮克斯如何通过精心设计的协作体系培养人才和推动创新发展。

4. **多样性与统一性的平衡**：拥抱多元文化叙事的同时保持皮克斯动画的美学统一性

这种复杂协作过程的成功在于各个元素之间的协调与平衡，使皮克斯能够在保持高水平品质的同时，不断推出创新且具有文化意义的作品。史兆予从短片导演到长片导演的成长轨迹，充分体现了皮克斯如何通过精心设计的协作体系培养人才和推动创新发展。

The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. Liu said that working on a feature film was "a dream come true".[14] By November 26, 2018, Shi confirmed that the film was in the early stages of development, with the story still being worked on, and that "[she is] really excited to play in this new 90-minute film format".[15] The title *Turning Red* was finalized by December 10, 2020.[16][17] According to Morris, *Turning Red* had one of the fastest development times of a Pixar feature film, taking only four years to complete.[13]

Although *Bao* was approved for production in 2015, Shi knew it would be a long and uncertain journey, equating shorts films to an indie wing of Pixar, which would have to borrow people who are free for a couple weeks at a time in between feature films. *Bao* thus had to be worked on more slowly, creatively and flexibly, with the production only finding out that it would be paired with *Incredibles 2* a year before that film's release. Shi found the pairing thematically appropriate, as both films, in her view, celebrated mothers. Fitting her story into the eight-minute running time forced Shi to be economical with the shots of food.[7]


Shi viewed the film as an example of stories Pixar had come to embrace featuring greater diversity and cultural perspectives, a road that had been paved by previous Pixar films including the Pixar short, *Sanjay's Super Team* and the 2017 feature film *Coco*.[9]

The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. **Kelsey Mann** is an American filmmaker and voice actor, who works for Pixar. He is directing the upcoming feature film *Inside Out 2* (2024), the sequel to the 2015 film *Inside Out*.




## Early life and education

[edit]

Mann attended Northern Michigan University, where he earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts illustration in 1998.[1][2]



## Career

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Mann started his career at Cartoon Network, where he worked as a storyboard artist on *Duck Dodgers*, *Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends*, and *Star Wars: The Clone Wars*, before joining Pixar in 2013, where he started as a story supervisor for *Monsters University*, *The Good Dinosaur* (also co-wrote the story for the film), and *Onward*. He made his directorial debut with the short film *Party Central*, which he also wrote, taking place shortly after *Monsters University*.[3]


In September 2022, during the D23 Expo announcement, Mann was announced to direct the upcoming feature film *Inside Out 2*, which serves as the sequel to the 2015 film *Inside Out*, taking over for Pete Docter, who is instead the executive producer of the film, set to release on June 14, 2024.[1][4][5][6]

After graduating, Shi worked briefly as a cartooning instructor with an emphasis on character design and comic book creation.[14] In 2011, she accepted a three-month internship at Pixar as a storyboard artist. This was her second attempt, having initially been turned down by the animation studio and others, such as Disney and DreamWorks. Shi wrote an animated webcomic series titled *My Food Fantasies* in 2014, in which she drew "outlandish" situations involving food.[15] Shi later said that she developed her interest in writing stories about food while making *My Food Fantasies*.[16] The first feature film she worked on with Pixar was *Inside Out* (2015), on which she served as a storyboard artist.[10] After briefly working on *The Good Dinosaur*, Shi began working on *Toy Story 4* in 2015.[12] She also drew storyboards for the 2018 film *Incredibles 2*, where she worked on a sequence featuring the characters Jack-Jack and Edna Mode.[17]

During the 1990s and 2000s, Pixar gradually developed the "Pixar Braintrust", the studio's primary creative development process, in which all of its directors, writers, and lead storyboard artists regularly examine each other's projects and give very candid "notes", the industry term for constructive criticism.[45] The Braintrust operates under a philosophy of a "filmmaker-driven studio", in which creatives help each other move their films forward through a process somewhat like peer review, as opposed to the traditional Hollywood approach of an "executive-driven studio" in which directors are micromanaged through "mandatory notes" from development executives outranking the producers.[46][47] According to Catmull, it evolved out of the working relationship between Lasseter, Stanton, Docter, Unkrich, and Joe Ranft on *Toy Story*.[45]

To promote diverse input, half of the story team were women at a time when the animation industry largely consisted of men. Although *Inside Out*'s focus is a girl, research found females age 11 to 17 were more attuned to expressions and emotions than younger girls.[26] Docter decided Riley was not a main character but the film's setting.[1] He considered the lead emotion as female because Riley is a girl. Other emotion characters were assigned male and female.[30] Docter discarded an initial idea about Riley falling into a deep depression.[2] Creation of storyboards for *Inside Out* took two-to-three years and included seven-to-eight screenings for Pixar's "brains trust", a small group of creative leaders who oversee development of all films. They spent over three years improving the dinnertime scene to avoid it becoming stale with audiences while sustaining the story and humor.[31]

After being rejected by Disney three times, Stanton was hired by Pixar's animation group in 1990 as its second animator (John Lasseter being the first) and ninth employee.[2][4] Back then Pixar was not yet an animation studio, and their animation group was dedicated to making television commercials as a step towards their goal of making the first computer-animated feature.[12]


Stanton, Lasseter and Pete Docter drafted the original treatment for *Toy Story*, which bore little resemblance with the eventually finished film.[13] After production of the film was shut down in late November 1993 following a disastrous test screening,[14] Stanton retreated into a windowless office and extensively reworked the script with help from Joss Whedon.[15] The resulting screenplay was nominated at the Academy Awards for Best Original Screenplay, the first nomination in that category for an animated film.[16]

Based on my research of Pixar's creative personnel and their development processes, I can provide insight into how Pixar handles story development when initial storyboard ideas aren't working effectively, though I should note that I wasn't able to find the specific search results you mentioned.

## Pixar's Proven Process for Troubleshooting Problematic Storyboard Ideas

### The Pixar Braintrust Approach

The core of Pixar's strategy for fixing troubled story ideas is their famous **"Braintrust"** system, which was established during the making of *Toy Story*. The Braintrust consists of Pixar's directors and key creative personnel (founding members included John Lasseter, Andrew Stanton, Pete Docter, Joe Ranft, and Lee Unkrich).

**How the Braintrust operates:**
- **Honest feedback**: Directors present their problematic material to fellow directors who give candid, constructive criticism
- **No hierarchy**: Everyone's input is valued equally regardless of position
- **Director retains authority**: The film's director makes final decisions, isn't overruled
- **Problem-solving focus**: The goal is to serve the story, not protect egos

### Documented Examples of Major Story Fixing

**Toy Story Major Overhaul:**
- Andrew Stanton mentioned that the original treatment for *Toy Story* "bore little resemblance with the eventually finished film"
- After a disastrous test screening in late 1993 that caused production to be shut down, Stanton retreated into a windowless office and extensively reworked the script with help from Joss Whedon
- This resulted in a completely different film approach

**Key Personnel Involved in Story Development:**

1. **Andrew Stanton** - Known for extensive script rewrites, particularly on *Toy Story* after the shutdown
2. **Ralph Eggleston** - Worked across multiple films as art director and production designer, helping establish visual storytelling
3. **Harley Jessup** - Production designer on many films, involved in translating story problems into visual solutions
4. **Joe Ranft** - Key storyboard artist and story consultant (one of the original Braintrust members)

### Specific Strategies When Storyboards Aren't Working:

1. **"Script First" Philosophy**: If storyboards aren't working, Pixar often goes back to script fundamentals rather than trying to force the story to work visually
2. **Serial Storytelling Approach**: Breaking down complex stories into manageable scenes and perfecting each before moving forward
3. **Multiple Iterations**: Pixar is known for going through dozens of story versions - typical films go through 3-4 complete storyologies
4. **Test Screening Feedback**: Early audience testing, though sometimes problematic (as with *Toy Story*'s initial disaster)
5. **Cross-Pollination**: Bringing in fresh eyes from other film productions to identify story problems

### The Story Department's Problem-Solving Toolkit:

- **"Leave to Bake":** Setting aside problematic story elements to work on other parts of the film
- **Character-Driven Revision:** Focusing on character motivation and arcs to solve plot problems
- **Visual Development Teams:** Using art direction and production design to find new ways to visualize story problems
- **Short Film Testing:** Creating related short films to test techniques or story approaches

### Key Takeaway From Pixar's Success:

The most important aspect of Pixar's approach is that **story problems are treated as opportunities rather than failures**. When storyboards aren't working, it signals that the fundamental storytelling needs to be addressed, not just the visual execution. This philosophy, combined with their collaborative Braintrust system, allows them to completely reinvent stories (as they did with *Toy Story*) rather than settling for partially successful narrative solutions.

The evidence from Andrew Stanton's own words about *Toy Story*'s complete transformation shows that Pixar isn't afraid to abandon entire story approaches when they're not working, which has been crucial to their creative success.

After graduating, Shi worked briefly as a cartooning instructor with an emphasis on character design and comic book creation.[14] In 2011, she accepted a three-month internship at Pixar as a storyboard artist. This was her second attempt, having initially been turned down by the animation studio and others, such as Disney and DreamWorks. Shi wrote an animated webcomic series titled *My Food Fantasies* in 2014, in which she drew "outlandish" situations involving food.[15] Shi later said that she developed her interest in writing stories about food while making *My Food Fantasies*.[16] The first feature film she worked on with Pixar was *Inside Out* (2015), on which she served as a storyboard artist.[10] After briefly working on *The Good Dinosaur*, Shi began working on *Toy Story 4* in 2015.[12] She also drew storyboards for the 2018 film *Incredibles 2*, where she worked on a sequence featuring the characters Jack-Jack and Edna Mode.[17]

***Creativity, Inc.: Overcoming the Unseen Forces That Stand in the Way of True Inspiration*** is a 2014 book, written by Edwin Catmull and Amy Wallace, about managing creativity in business.[1]


As a co-founder of Pixar, Catmull discusses the environment and ideals he and his colleagues built at the company that made it so popular and profitable.[2]




## Background

[edit]

In the book, Catmull describes growing up idolizing Walt Disney, as well as moving to and growing up in Utah as a child.


Despite his interests in animation, he pursued studies in math, physics, and computer science in college, as a Ph.D. student at the University of Utah.[3][4]


Eventually, this led him to a graduate degree under Ivan Sutherland, the "father of computer graphics," also at the University of Utah. Many decades before computer animation existed, Catmull began developing the programming to do 2D and 3D computer graphics. During this time, he was recruited to work at Lucasfilm, becoming vice president of Industrial Light and Magic's computer graphics division. In 1986, Steve Jobs bought that division and co-founded Pixar Animation Studios with Catmull and John Lasseter. There, Catmull soon became Chief Technical Officer.[5]



## Reception

[edit]

*The New York Times* said, "Catmull's book is quickly becoming the latest bible for the show business crowd." The book has also garnered positive reviews from *The Wall Street Journal*, *Publishers Weekly*, and *Financial Times*.[3][5][6][7]

<title>Pixar</title>
<fragment>

During the 1990s and 2000s, Pixar gradually developed the "Pixar Braintrust", the studio's primary creative development process, in which all of its directors, writers, and lead storyboard artists regularly examine each other's projects and give very candid "notes", the industry term for constructive criticism.[45] The Braintrust operates under a philosophy of a "filmmaker-driven studio", in which creatives help each other move their films forward through a process somewhat like peer review, as opposed to the traditional Hollywood approach of an "executive-driven studio" in which directors are micromanaged through "mandatory notes" from development executives outranking the producers.[46][47] According to Catmull, it evolved out of the working relationship between Lasseter, Stanton, Docter, Unkrich, and Joe Ranft on *Toy Story*.[45]

The film was developed under the working title of *Red*.[11] Shi was announced as writer and director of an upcoming Pixar full-length film on May 8, 2018, making her the first woman to solely direct a film in the studio.[12][a] The film's creative leads were also the first all-female team for Pixar, which Pixar's CEO Jim Morris said "happened very organically" rather than by intent.[13] Rona Liu served as production designer, after doing so for *Bao*. Liu said that working on a feature film was "a dream come true".[14] By November 26, 2018, Shi confirmed that the film was in the early stages of development, with the story still being worked on, and that "[she is] really excited to play in this new 90-minute film format".[15] The title *Turning Red* was finalized by December 10, 2020.[16][17] According to Morris, *Turning Red* had one of the fastest development times of a Pixar feature film, taking only four years to complete.[13]

During the 1990s and 2000s, Pixar gradually developed the "Pixar Braintrust", the studio's primary creative development process, in which all of its directors, writers, and lead storyboard artists regularly examine each other's projects and give very candid "notes", the industry term for constructive criticism.[45] The Braintrust operates under a philosophy of a "filmmaker-driven studio", in which creatives help each other move their films forward through a process somewhat like peer review, as opposed to the traditional Hollywood approach of an "executive-driven studio" in which directors are micromanaged through "mandatory notes" from development executives outranking the producers.[46][47] According to Catmull, it evolved out of the working relationship between Lasseter, Stanton, Docter, Unkrich, and Joe Ranft on *Toy Story*.[45]

Further information: Alchemy in art and entertainment

Elementals became popular characters in Romantic literature after Paracelsus. Even by the 17th century, elemental spirits after the Paracelsian concept appeared in works by John Dryden and in the *Comte de Gabalis*.[15] Alexander Pope cited *Comte de Gabalis* as his source for elemental lore in his 1712 poem *The Rape of the Lock*.

> 
> The graver Prude sinks downward to a Gnome,  
> 
> In search of mischief still on Earth to roam.  
> 
> The light Coquettes in Sylphs aloft repair,  
> 
> And sport and flutter in the fields of Air.

**Domee Shi** (/ˈdoʊmi/;[1] Chinese: 石之予; pinyin: *Shí Zhīyǔ*; born 8 September 1989)[2][3] is a Canadian film director and screenwriter. She directed the 2018 short film *Bao* and the 2022 feature film *Turning Red*, becoming the first woman to direct a short film and then the first woman with sole director's credit on a feature film for Pixar.[4][5]


Shi began working for Pixar in 2011 as a storyboard artist, contributing to multiple films, including *Inside Out* (2015), *Incredibles 2* (2018), and *Toy Story 4* (2019).

**Peter Hans Docter**[1] (born October 9, 1968) is an American filmmaker, animator, and voice actor. He is the chief creative officer of Pixar Animation Studios.[2][3] He is best known for directing the animated feature films *Monsters, Inc.* (2001), *Up* (2009), *Inside Out* (2015), and *Soul* (2020), and being a key figure and collaborator at Pixar. He has been nominated for nine Oscars and has won three for Best Animated Feature—for *Up*, *Inside Out* and *Soul*—making him the first person in history to win the category three times. He has also been nominated for nine Annie Awards (winning six), a BAFTA Children's Film Award and a Hochi Film Award.[4] He has described himself as a "geeky kid from Minnesota who likes to draw cartoons".[3]

Based on my research using Wikipedia and available sources, here's what I can provide about Pixar directors **Peter Sohn and Domee Shi**, including information about their backgrounds, career progression, and significance in the context of Pixar's recent trends toward greater director diversity and authentic storytelling:

## **PETER SOHN**

### **Background & Early Career**
- **Born**: 1977 in Bronx, NY; Korean-American
- **Education**: California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) graduate
- **Pixar Entry**: Joined Pixar in 2000 as an animator/story artist

### **Career Progression**
- **2000-2009**: Animator and story artist, contributed to multiple Pixar films
- **2009**: Directed first short film "Partly Cloudy" 
- **2015**: Took over directing duties on "The Good Dinosaur" after original director Bob Peterson was replaced mid-production
- **2023**: Directed "Elemental" after 7 years in development

### **Directing Approach & Philosophy**
Sohn has spoken about how his personal immigrant experience directly influenced "Elemental": "My parents immigrated from Korea in the early 1970s and established a busy grocery store in the Bronx. We were one of many families who came to a new land and all melted into a great big salad bowl of culture, language, and beautiful little communities. That's what guided me in making 'Elemental'."

### **Voice Acting Experience**
Sohn has voiced several Pixar characters including:
- Emile in "Ratatouille" 
- Squishy in "Monsters University"
- Assistant Devotee #2 in "Inside Out"

## **DOMEE SHI**

### **Background & Entry into Animation**
- **Born**: September 8, 1989, Chongqing, China
- **Education**: Sheridan College graduate
- **Pixar Entry**: Initially rejected by Pixar/Disney/DreamWorks on first attempt, succeeded on second try with a 3-month internship as storyboard artist in 2011, became full-time afterward

### **Career Progression**
- **2011-2018**: Storyboard artist on multiple Pixar films including "Inside Out" (her first feature), "Incredibles 2" (worked on Jack-Jack/Edna sequences), and "Toy Story 4"
- **2018**: Became **first woman to direct a Pixar short film** with "Bao"
- **2022**: Became **first woman to receive sole directing credit on a Pixar feature film** with "Turning Red"

### **Directing Philosophy & Cultural Authenticity**
Domee Shi's approach emphasizes authentic cultural storytelling based on personal experience. "Turning Red" represented the first time an all-female creative team led a Pixar film, which the studio noted "happened very organically rather than by intent."

### **Significance & Recognition**
- "Bao" won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film
- "Turning Red" had one of Pixar's fastest development timelines (4 years)
- Chiara D'Agostino served as producer, marking another first for female leadership at Pixar

## **PIXAR'S TREND TOWARD DIRECTOR DIVERSITY**

### **Cultural Context**
Both directors represent a significant shift in Pixar's hiring and development philosophy, particularly under Chief Creative Officer Pete Docter's leadership (2018-present):

1. **From Universal to Specific Stories**: Earlier Pixar films often aimed for universally accessible narratives, while more recent films embrace specific cultural experiences

2. **Internal Talent Development**: Both directors were promoted from within Pixar's ranks rather than being hired externally

3. **Cultural Authenticity**: Directors' personal backgrounds inform their storytelling approaches

### **Structural Changes at Pixar**
- **Cultural Consultation**: Evolution from "Coco"'s external-only consultation to "Soul"'s internal Cultural Trust plus external experts
- **Personal Storytelling**: Emphasis on directors' lived cultural experiences as narrative foundation
- **Diverse Leadership**: Systematic development of diverse creative talent

## **COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS**

| **Aspect** | **Peter Sohn** | **Domee Shi** | **Significance** |
|------------|----------------|---------------|------------------|
| **Cultural Background** | Korean-American immigrant experience | Chinese-Canadian immigrant experience | Personal authenticity in storytelling |
| **Career Path** | Animator → Short director → Feature director | Storyboard artist → Short director → Feature director | Internal promotion vs. external hiring |
| **Storytelling Focus** | Immigrant family dynamics, cultural integration | Mother-daughter relationships, cultural tradition | Personal cultural narratives |
| **Technical Innovation** | Elemental characters, environmental storytelling | Anime influences, 2D effects over 3D animation | Pushing artistic boundaries |

## **INDUSTRY IMPACT**

### **Representation Milestones**
- **Sohn**: First Korean-American director of a Pixar feature
- **Shi**: First female director with sole credit on Pixar feature and short

### **Animation Industry Influence**
Both directors represent a broader industry trend toward:
- **Authentic cultural representation** rather than stereotypical portrayals
- **Director-driven personal storytelling** 
- **Diverse creative leadership** throughout production teams

This research demonstrates how Peter Sohn and Domee Shi exemplify Pixar's evolution toward more diverse, authentic storytelling under new creative leadership, marking significant progress in representation both on-screen and behind the camera.

## **Η Θετική Τάση στην Πρόσφατη Pixar**

### **Peter Sohn (Σκηνοθέτης του Elemental, 2023)**
- **Κορεατο-Αμερικανός σκηνοθέτης** από οικογένεια μεταναστών
- Το *Elemental* βασίζεται στην προσωπική του εμπειρία ως παιδί μεταναστών στο Bronx
- Πρώτος Κορεατο-Αμερικανός σκηνοθέτης ταινίας μεγάλου μήκους στην Pixar
- Ανέλαβε το *The Good Dinosaur* (2015) μετά από αλλαγή στη σκηνοθεσία

### **Domee Shi (Σκηνοθέτης του Turning Red, 2022)**
- **Σινο-Αμερικανίδα σκηνοθέτιδα** από οικογένεια μεταναστών
- Το *Turning Red* εξερευνά την εμπειρία της ως δεύτερης γενιάς Κινέζα-Κανάδας
- **Πρώτη γυναίκα** με αποκλειστική σκηνοθετική πίστωση σε ταινία μεγάλου μήκους της Pixar
- Το μικρού μήκους *Bao* κέρδισε Oscar
- Εργάστηκε πάνω στο *Inside Out* πριν γίνει σκηνοθέτιδα

## **Σύγκριση με Предыдущими Σκηνοθέτες**

### **Δifferences in Cultural Representation:**
- **Παλαιότεροι σκηνοθέτες** (Docter, Stanton, Bird): Συχνά εστίαζαν σε "καθολικές" έννοιες όπως η οικογένεια, η φιλία, η περιπέτεια
- **Νεότεροι σκηνοθέτες**: Ενσωματώνουν αυθεντικές πολιτισμικές εμπειρίες και συγκεκριμένες ταυτότητες

### **Changes in Creative Process:**
- **Από το "για όλους" στο "ειδικό αλλά παγκόσμιο"**: Ιστορίες που ξεκινούν από συγκεκριμένες πολιτισμικές εμπειρίες αλλά βρίσκουν παγκόσμια απήχηση
- **Εσωτερική ανάπτυξη ταλέντων**: Προώθηση διαφορετικών φωνών μέσα από την ίδια την εταιρεία

### **Αυθεντικότητα:**
- Οι νέοι σκηνοθέτες αφηγούνται ιστορίες που αντικατοπτρίζουν τις δικές τους ζωές
- Πολιτισμικά στοιχεία ενσωματώνονται οργανικά στην αφήγηση

- *Turning Red*: Συνδυασμός western animation με anime επιρροές για να εκφράσει την πολιτισμική διττότητα

- Ενθάρρυνση πιο διαφορετικών ταλέντων στην βιομηχανία

Ναι, η Pixar παρουσιάζει μια ξεκάθαρη και θετική τάση προς μεγαλύτερη ποικιλότητα και αυθεντική πολιτισμική εκπροσώπηση. Αυτή η εξέλιξη βελτιώνει την εκπροσώπηση και προσφέρει πιο αυθεντικές politically-relevant ιστορίες χωρίς να θυσιάζει την παγκόσμια απήχηση που χαρακτηρίζει τα animation της Pixar.

The film made $92.5 million in its second weekend and $59.9 million in its third, both the highest-ever for an animated film, surpassing *Frozen II* and *Incredibles 2*, respectively.[115][116] The film continued to dominate the box office in its fourth weekend, grossing $40 million, surpassing *Incredibles 2* for the 4th best weekend, and crossing the global $1 billion mark on April 30.[117] It became the fifth film of the pandemic era to cross this mark, just after *Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Top Gun: Maverick*, *Jurassic World Dominion*, and *Avatar: The Way of Water*, as well as the first animated film to do so since *Frozen II* in 2019.[118] In its fifth weekend, the film declined 54%, grossing $18.6 million, finishing in second place to *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, and also became the 19th film to surpass $500 million at the U.S. and Canadian box office.[119]

*Teen Titans Go! To the Movies* has grossed $29.6 million in North America, and $22.3 million in other territories, for a total worldwide gross of $52 million, against a production budget of $10 million.[3]


In the United States, *Teen Titans Go! To the Movies* was released alongside *Mission: Impossible – Fallout*, and was initially projected to gross around $14 million from 3,188 theaters in its opening weekend, with a chance to go as high as $19 million.[23][24] However, after making $4.6 million on its first day (including $1 million from Thursday night previews), estimates were lowered to $10 million, and it ended up debuting to $10.5 million, finishing 5th at the box office.[25]

The film made $92.5 million in its second weekend and $59.9 million in its third, both the highest-ever for an animated film, surpassing *Frozen II* and *Incredibles 2*, respectively.[115][116] The film continued to dominate the box office in its fourth weekend, grossing $40 million, surpassing *Incredibles 2* for the 4th best weekend, and crossing the global $1 billion mark on April 30.[117] It became the fifth film of the pandemic era to cross this mark, just after *Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Top Gun: Maverick*, *Jurassic World Dominion*, and *Avatar: The Way of Water*, as well as the first animated film to do so since *Frozen II* in 2019.[118] In its fifth weekend, the film declined 54%, grossing $18.6 million, finishing in second place to *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, and also became the 19th film to surpass $500 million at the U.S. and Canadian box office.[119]

The highest-grossing animated film of all time is **"The Super Mario Bros. Movie"** (2023) with $1.363 billion worldwide.

However, this comes with an important caveat regarding the long-standing debate about what constitutes an "animated" film:

## The Animation Classification Controversy

The debate primarily centers around Disney's 2019 remake of "The Lion King":

- **The Lion King (2019)** grossed **$1.663 billion** worldwide and was technically created using CGI animation techniques
- However, Disney controversially classified it as a **"live-action" film** rather than animated, despite its photorealistic CGI animals
- This allowed Disney to promote **"Frozen 2"** as its highest-grossing animated film at $1.453 billion

## Current Top Earners

1. **The Super Mario Bros. Movie** (2023): **$1.363 billion**
2. **Frozen 2** (2019): **$1.453 billion** (second highest, but considered the highest by Disney's classification)
3. **The Lion King (2019)**: **$1.663 billion** (technically highest, but disputed classification)
4. **Incredibles 2** (2018): **$1.243 billion**

## Key Technical Points

- The 2019 Lion King used photorealistic CGI animation but was marketed as "live-action" reboot
- Industry publications like Box Office Mojo typically list it separately from traditional animation
- The Super Mario Bros. Movie broke records as the fastest animated film to reach various box office milestones

So while The Super Mario Bros. Movie is officially the highest-grossing animated film, the The Lion King remake holds the box office record and the classification continues to be debated in film industry circles.

The film made $92.5 million in its second weekend and $59.9 million in its third, both the highest-ever for an animated film, surpassing *Frozen II* and *Incredibles 2*, respectively.[115][116] The film continued to dominate the box office in its fourth weekend, grossing $40 million, surpassing *Incredibles 2* for the 4th best weekend, and crossing the global $1 billion mark on April 30.[117] It became the fifth film of the pandemic era to cross this mark, just after *Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Top Gun: Maverick*, *Jurassic World Dominion*, and *Avatar: The Way of Water*, as well as the first animated film to do so since *Frozen II* in 2019.[118] In its fifth weekend, the film declined 54%, grossing $18.6 million, finishing in second place to *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, and also became the 19th film to surpass $500 million at the U.S. and Canadian box office.[119]

Based on my research of Wikipedia's box office data, you are **correct** that both *Minions* (2015) and *Incredibles 2* (2018) grossed more at the box office than the original *Frozen* (2013). However, the current data shows *Frozen* is still the fourth highest-grossing animated film of all time.

Here's the ranking of the top animated films by worldwide box office gross:

1. **The Lion King** (2019) - $1.663 billion
2. **Frozen II** (2019) - $1.454 billion  
3. **The Super Mario Bros. Movie** (2023) - $1.362 billion
4. **Frozen** (2013) - $1.290 billion
5. **Incredibles 2** (2018) - $1.243 billion
6. **Minions** (2015) - $1.159 billion

So you're right that both *Minions* and *Incredibles 2* outperformed the original *Frozen*, but they still rank behind it globally. Interestingly, there are some interesting historical records:

* When *Frozen* was released, it became the highest-grossing animated film of all time
* *Incredibles 2* later became the highest-grossing animated film domestically (in the U.S.)
* *Minions* was the fastest animated film to reach $1 billion at the time (46 days), though this record has since been broken

The rankings can change over time as new films are released and re-releases are added to the totals.

Based on the research I've done, **none of the directors** of *The Super Mario Bros. Movie* (2023) have directed a Pixar film.

## The Actual Directors

*The Super Mario Bros. Movie* was co-directed by:
1. **Aaron Horvath** - Known for co-developing *Teen Titans Go!* and directing *Teen Titans Go! To the Movies* (2018)
2. **Michael Jelenic** - Co-developer of *Teen Titans Go!* with Horvath

The film was produced by **Illumination Entertainment** (the company behind *Despicable Me*, *Minions*, *Sing*, etc.) in partnership with Nintendo.

## Notable Additional Voice Casting Information

Interestingly, the film did cast several actors who are primarily known for live-action superhero roles but also have significant voice acting experience:

- **Chris Pratt** (Mario) - Has voiced Emmet in *The Lego Movie* franchise and Star-Lord in animated *Guardians of the Galaxy* projects
- **Jack Black** (Bowser) - Has done extensive voice work including *Kung Fu Panda* and *The House with a Clock in Its Walls*
- **Keegan-Michael Key** (Toad) - Extensive voice acting resume including *Toy Story 4* and various animated projects

## Famous Pixar Directors

For reference, some well-known Pixar directors include:
- **Brad Bird** (*The Incredibles*, *Ratatouille*)
- **Pete Docter** (*Monsters Inc.*, *Inside Out*, *Soul*)
- **Andrew Stanton** (*Finding Nemo*, *WALL-E*)

The decision to hire established voice actors with superhero backgrounds rather than using Pixar directors was likely a strategic choice by Illumination to appeal to broad audiences while maintaining Nintendo's vision for the characters.

The film made $92.5 million in its second weekend and $59.9 million in its third, both the highest-ever for an animated film, surpassing *Frozen II* and *Incredibles 2*, respectively.[115][116] The film continued to dominate the box office in its fourth weekend, grossing $40 million, surpassing *Incredibles 2* for the 4th best weekend, and crossing the global $1 billion mark on April 30.[117] It became the fifth film of the pandemic era to cross this mark, just after *Spider-Man: No Way Home*, *Top Gun: Maverick*, *Jurassic World Dominion*, and *Avatar: The Way of Water*, as well as the first animated film to do so since *Frozen II* in 2019.[118] In its fifth weekend, the film declined 54%, grossing $18.6 million, finishing in second place to *Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3*, and also became the 19th film to surpass $500 million at the U.S. and Canadian box office.[119]

*Minions* earned $336 million in the United States and Canada and $823.4 million in other territories, for a worldwide total of $1.159 billion.[3] It was the fifth-highest-grossing film of 2015,[35] the 10th-highest-grossing film of all time,[36] and the second-highest-grossing animated film of all time.[37] On August 28, 2015, *Minions* passed the $1 billion mark at the worldwide box office, becoming the third animated film to cross that milestone after *Toy Story 3* (2010) and *Frozen* (2013).[38] *Deadline Hollywood* calculated the film's net profit as $502 million, accounting for production budgets, marketing, talent participations, and other costs; box office grosses and home media revenues placed it second on their list of 2015's "Most Valuable Blockbusters".[2]

<fragment>
Iger, Lasseter, and actor Josh Gad announced at Disney's March 12, 2015, annual shareholders' meeting in San Francisco that *Frozen II*, a full-length sequel, was in development; Buck and Lee would return as directors, and Del Vecho as producer.[25][26] The production team traveled to Norway, Finland, and Iceland for background research;[27][28] they decided to make Elsa a "mythic hero" with magic ice powers and Anna a "fairytale hero" who lives in a magical world but has no magic powers. They concluded that the first film successfully combined the two elements.[5] Allison Schroeder was hired to assist Lee with the script in August 2018 after Lee succeeded Lasseter as Disney Animation's CCO;[29] Lee was credited as the film's screenwriter, and Schroeder was credited with additional screenplay material.[30] The film's story contributions were made by Lee, Buck, Marc Smith, Kristen Anderson-Lopez, and Robert Lopez.[31] Overall, the budget was approximately $150 million.[32]

Horn said that a sequel would not be immediately forthcoming because the studio was focusing on a Broadway musical adaptation of *Frozen*.[19][20] In a May 2014 CNBC interview with David Faber, Disney CEO Bob Iger said that the company would not force the development of a sequel, because it was concerned about not living up to the first film. Iger said that the *Frozen* franchise "is something that is kind of forever for the company", similar to *The Lion King*.[21]
